title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 31–32
description: Curated B2 transport, travel, accommodation and holiday-description vocabulary, with original example sentences and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets and learning topics were checked against its study pages, illustrations, exercises and answer key. All example sentences and teaching notes are independently written; original exercise passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Study text, transport and holiday tables, holiday messages, sample collocations, exercise pages, language notes and answer-key entries reviewed for relevant vocabulary and usage.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British English IPA for words and short expressions where confidence is high; longer and uncertain transcriptions are omitted rather than guessed. Some regional pronunciation variants are not shown.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except the Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Review of source study and exercise pages with answer key; editorial and linguistic review; offline JSON schema, IDs, origin and audio-target checks. No browser TTS, recognition or live app import testing performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings are supplied. The empty audio paths do not establish live TTS or VocabLab compatibility testing, and travel descriptions are examples of language usage rather than current transport service data.

units.title: Unit 31 — Travel
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 31. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify transport types, vehicle parts, transport personnel and facilities used by road, rail, sea and air.
Distinguish journey, trip, travel, voyage and flight, including countability and standard collocations.
Discuss disrupted journeys, airline arrangements and motion sickness using natural travel expressions.
Use on time for punctuality and distinguish it from in time.

sectionsChecked: A: Road, rail, sea and air transport table and associated professions, facilities and parts
B: Journey, trip, travel and voyage; countability and trip collocations
C: Flight delays, overnight accommodation, standby passengers, turbulence and sailing; common mistakes
Exercises 31.1–31.4 and answer key including transport sorting and travel-blog language

items.example: We took a coach to the coastal town because the train was expensive.
items.note: In road travel, a coach is a bus designed for longer journeys.

items.example: The old town has a tram that runs through the main square.
items.note: A public vehicle that follows tracks in the street.

items.example: The delivery van stopped outside the shop.
items.note: Usually smaller than a lorry and used to transport goods or people.

items.example: A broken-down lorry blocked one lane of the motorway.
items.note: British English; American English commonly uses truck.

items.example: Put the suitcases in the boot before we set off.
items.note: The storage space at the back of a car in British English; American English: trunk.

items.example: Keep both hands on the steering wheel on narrow mountain roads.
items.note: The wheel used to control a vehicle's direction.

items.example: Motorists were warned about ice on the roads.
items.note: A person who drives a car; common in reports and notices.

items.example: A mechanic inspected the engine after the car stopped.
items.note: A person trained to repair vehicles or machines.

items.example: The visiting director arrived with a chauffeur.
items.note: A professional driver, often employed to drive one person or group.

items.example: We stopped at a petrol station to fill up the car.
items.note: British English; American English: gas station.

items.example: Our car broke down just outside the city.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb for a vehicle or machine that stops working.

items.example: We called a breakdown service when the engine failed.
items.note: Roadside assistance for a vehicle that has stopped working.

items.example: The high-speed train cut the journey to just two hours.
items.note: A train built to travel at very high speeds.

items.example: We caught the express instead of the stopping service.
items.note: As a noun here, an express is a train with few stops.

items.example: Our tickets included beds in a sleeping car.
items.note: A railway carriage equipped for overnight accommodation.

items.pt: vagão-bar; serviço de refeições no trem
items.example: The buffet was closed, so we brought our own sandwiches.
items.note: In this rail context, a counter or carriage that serves refreshments.

items.example: Our seats were in the last coach of the train.
items.note: Also means a railway carriage, as well as a long-distance bus.

items.example: The conductor announced the next station.
items.note: A member of staff who assists passengers, sometimes checking tickets.

items.pt: fiscal de bilhetes; cobrador de passagens
items.example: The ticket collector asked to see our passes.
items.note: A person who checks passengers' travel tickets.

items.example: The train to Oxford leaves from platform five.
items.note: The raised area beside a railway track where passengers board.

items.example: A seat reservation is recommended on busy trains.
items.note: An advance arrangement to have a particular seat.

items.pt: navio de passageiros de grande porte
items.example: An ocean liner used to carry passengers across the Atlantic.
items.note: A large passenger ship; the term is often associated with historic sea routes.

items.example: The ferry takes passengers and cars across the channel.
items.note: A boat or ship making regular crossings, often with vehicles.

items.example: They hired a yacht for a week around the islands.
items.note: A sailing or motor boat used for pleasure.

items.example: Passengers gathered on deck to watch the sunset.
items.note: An outdoor or indoor horizontal level of a ship.

items.pt: ponte de comando de um navio
items.example: The captain directed the ship from the bridge.
items.note: Here, the control area of a ship, not a structure over a river.

items.example: We crossed the gangway to board the ferry.
items.note: A walkway used when passengers board or leave a ship.

items.example: The captain announced a change to the sailing route.
items.note: The person in charge of a ship or aircraft.

items.example: A steward showed us to our cabin.
items.note: A staff member who looks after passengers; stewardess is a traditional female form.

items.example: The ship returned to port before the storm arrived.
items.note: A place where ships arrive, leave and load or unload.

items.example: They booked a quiet cabin below deck.
items.note: A small private room on a ship; also used for aircraft interiors.

items.example: My grandparents went on a cruise around the Baltic Sea.
items.note: A holiday on a ship that visits several destinations.

items.example: Several aircraft were waiting to depart.
items.note: Both singular and plural can be aircraft, without an -s ending.

items.pt: avião a jato de grande porte
items.example: The airline retired its last jumbo jet last year.
items.note: A very large jet aircraft, originally especially a Boeing 747.

items.example: A rescue helicopter landed near the mountain hut.
items.note: An aircraft lifted by rotating blades.

items.example: Only authorised personnel may enter the cockpit.
items.note: The area where pilots control an aircraft.

items.example: My seat was directly above the wing.
items.note: The flat structure that generates lift when an aircraft moves.

items.example: She prefers an aisle seat so she can stand up easily.
items.note: The s is silent; used in aircraft, trains, theatres and shops.

items.example: Ground staff helped passengers find a new departure gate.
items.note: Airport workers who support flights and passengers on the ground.

items.example: The cabin crew checked that everyone had fastened their seat belts.
items.note: The flight attendants who look after people in an aircraft.

items.example: An air traffic controller directed the incoming aircraft.
items.note: A professional responsible for the safe movement of aircraft.

items.example: We visited the duty-free shop after passing security.
items.note: A shop at an airport or international travel terminal selling eligible goods without certain taxes.

items.example: Our flight departs from the new terminal.
items.note: A building where air passengers check in and arrive or depart.

items.example: The aircraft waited near the runway for clearance.
items.note: The strip of ground used for aircraft take-off and landing.

items.example: You need to pass through security before reaching the gates.
items.note: In airports, the checks for dangerous or prohibited items.

items.pt: viagem; trajeto, especialmente de um lugar a outro
items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: The journey home took longer because of heavy traffic.
items.note: A countable trip from one place to another; often used for longer or difficult travel.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: We planned a short trip to the seaside.
items.note: Countable and often shorter than a journey; can be for work or pleasure.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: She is away on a business trip until Friday.
items.note: Say business trip, not business journey.

items.pt: fazer um passeio; sair em uma viagem
items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: Our class went on a trip to a nature reserve.
items.note: Often suggests an organised excursion or outing.

items.pt: fazer uma viagem; dar um passeio
items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: We decided to take a trip to a nearby island.
items.note: Can describe an independently planned journey.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: Travel can be tiring when you have a tight schedule.
items.note: As a noun, travel is generally uncountable: not a travel.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: I usually travel by train when I visit my family.
items.note: As a verb, travel can be followed by by plus transport method.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: The research vessel began a voyage across the Pacific.
items.note: Countable; more formal than trip or journey when referring to sea travel.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: Learning another language can become a voyage of discovery.
items.note: A figurative expression for an experience full of new understanding.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: They chose to hitch-hike through several small towns.
items.note: Travel by accepting lifts from passing drivers; often written hitchhike.

items.section: B · Journey, trip, travel and voyage
items.example: The flight from Lisbon takes around three hours.
items.note: A countable journey in an aircraft.

items.example: Our train was severely delayed after a signal failure.
items.note: A strong adverb–adjective collocation for a serious delay.

items.example: The evening flight was cancelled because of snow.
items.note: Past participle of cancel; used when an arranged service will not operate.

items.pt: preso no aeroporto, sem conseguir sair
items.example: We were stuck at the airport when all departures stopped.
items.note: Stuck means unable to leave or move on as planned.

items.example: The airline put us up at a hotel near the airport.
items.note: Put someone up means provide accommodation, often temporarily.

items.pt: na lista de espera; aguardando vaga
items.example: They put me on standby for the first flight the next morning.
items.note: A place is offered only if space becomes available.

items.example: We managed to get a seat on the earlier train.
items.note: Common expression for securing an available place on transport.

items.example: Despite heavy rain, the coach arrived on time.
items.note: Means punctually; in time means early enough for a purpose.

items.example: There was mild turbulence as the plane approached the mountains.
items.note: Irregular air movement that can make an aircraft shake.

items.example: The pilot apologised for the bumpy landing.
items.note: An aircraft landing that feels uneven or jolting.

items.example: I felt airsick during the descent.
items.note: Sick because of movement during air travel.

items.example: She carries medication for airsickness when she flies.
items.note: The noun; a more formal alternative to getting airsick.

items.pt: descompensação de fuso horário; jet lag
items.example: The jetlag made it hard to sleep on my first night home.
items.note: Tiredness and disrupted sleep after crossing time zones; often written jet lag.

items.example: The journey ran smoothly despite the busy station.
items.note: A collocation for events happening without difficulty.

items.example: We waited for our baggage at the arrivals hall.
items.note: Uncountable; similar to luggage, and used for checked bags.

items.example: Our plane took off just after sunrise.
items.note: Intransitive for a plane leaving the ground; noun: take-off.

items.example: A customs officer checked the contents of our suitcase.
items.note: A border official concerned with goods entering or leaving a country.

items.example: The boat struggled to make progress in the rough sea.
items.note: The opposite of a calm sea.

items.example: The calm sea made the crossing comfortable.
items.note: Water with little wind or wave movement.

items.example: He gets seasick whenever he travels by small boat.
items.note: Sick because of a boat's movement.

items.example: Seasickness ruined part of their trip.
items.note: The noun describing illness caused by the movement of a boat.

items.example: There were twelve crew members on board.
items.note: Used for people present on a ship, plane or other vehicle.

items.example: Each crew member had a specific safety responsibility.
items.note: A person who works as part of a ship's or aircraft's crew.

items.example: It took me several days to get over the jetlag.
items.note: Get over something can mean recover from an illness or unpleasant experience.

items.example: Airport staff went on strike during the holiday season.
items.note: An established expression for workers stopping work together in a labour dispute.

items.example: I enquired about the last bus to the village.
items.note: British enquire often means ask for information; inquire is also used, especially in US English.

units.title: Unit 32 — Holidays
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 32. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Name different types of holiday, places to stay and related accommodation facilities.
Describe remote settings, holiday experiences and practical travel difficulties with precise adjectives.
Recognise promotional language and natural adjective–noun collocations used in holiday brochures.
Connect key descriptive adjectives with their related nouns and verbs.

sectionsChecked: A: Holiday accommodation and holiday types
B: Holiday-message descriptions of landscapes, roads, buildings and experiences
C: Brochure-style adjective–noun combinations and register
Exercises 32.1–32.4 and answer key including word-family forms

items.pt: área de camping; local para acampar
items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: The campsite had showers and a small kitchen.
items.note: A designated place for tents and sometimes caravans.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: We pitched a tent beside the river before dark.
items.note: Pitch is the usual verb for setting up a tent.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: They spent the summer travelling in a caravan.
items.note: In British English, a wheeled home pulled by a vehicle; American English often says trailer.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: A self-catering apartment gave us the freedom to cook our own meals.
items.note: Accommodation where guests prepare their own food; self-catering flat is also used.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: We found a family-run guesthouse near the beach.
items.note: Generally smaller and with fewer services than a hotel.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: The youth hostel offered shared rooms at a low price.
items.note: Budget accommodation often with shared bedrooms and facilities.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: I slept in the lower bunk bed because I dislike heights.
items.note: One of two or more beds arranged vertically.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: They booked a package holiday with flights and a hotel included.
items.note: A holiday sold for a combined price, usually booked in advance.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: We went on a cruise with stops in four ports.
items.note: A holiday spent travelling on a ship and visiting destinations.

items.pt: fazer uma parada durante o trajeto
items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: The ship stopped off at a small island for a few hours.
items.note: Make a short visit somewhere on the way to another destination.

items.pt: turismo para conhecer atrações e pontos turísticos
items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: We spent the afternoon sightseeing in the old district.
items.note: Visiting notable places for pleasure; often go sightseeing.

items.section: A · Places to stay and holiday types
items.example: An adventure holiday can include hiking and kayaking.
items.note: A holiday focused on unusual or exciting activities, sometimes involving risk.

items.pt: sair da rotina; viajar para descansar
items.example: We wanted to get away from the city for the weekend.
items.note: Leave your usual environment, often for rest or enjoyment.

items.example: The cottage was in a remote valley without mobile reception.
items.note: Far from populated places and services.

items.pt: estrada sinuosa; estrada cheia de curvas
items.example: A winding road led through the hills to the village.
items.note: Winding is pronounced /ˈwaɪndɪŋ/ in this sense; full of bends.

items.pt: zona rural ao redor; paisagem campestre circundante
items.example: We went cycling through the surrounding countryside.
items.note: The rural land around a particular place.

items.example: Crossing the suspension bridge was terrifying in the wind.
items.note: Something that causes great fear; stronger than frightening.

items.example: The climb was tiring but worthwhile for the view.
items.note: Worth the time or effort; often after be or make something worthwhile.

items.example: Our first trip abroad was a memorable holiday.
items.note: Memorable is strongly associated with occasions and experiences.

items.example: The guide gave a fascinating account of the city's history.
items.note: Extremely interesting or engaging.

items.example: The museum has an impressive collection of paintings.
items.note: Something that makes a strong favourable impact.

items.example: We spent a delightful afternoon in the gardens.
items.note: Especially pleasant or charming.

items.example: The hotel was inconvenient for public transport.
items.note: Not easy or practical to reach or use in the circumstances.

items.example: The restaurant served exceptional local food.
items.note: Unusually good in positive descriptions; not simply ordinary or typical.

items.example: The holiday brochure made the resort sound irresistible.
items.note: Advertising material describing holidays and accommodation, often with persuasive language.

items.example: The cliff-top path offered breathtaking views of the sea.
items.note: Breathtaking commonly combines with views and scenery.

items.example: The mountains provided breathtaking scenery throughout the walk.
items.note: Scenery is uncountable; breathtaking is a strong promotional adjective.

items.example: Guests have exclusive access to a private garden.
items.note: Access limited to a particular group.

items.example: Membership of the exclusive club requires an invitation.
items.note: A club that restricts entry or membership.

items.example: The rafting trip included an exhilarating ride through the rapids.
items.note: Exhilarating means causing strong excitement and energy.

items.example: The beach offered an exhilarating walk in the sea breeze.
items.note: An energetic experience that makes someone feel lively.

items.example: The photographer chose an exotic location for the shoot.
items.note: Exotic suggests a place that feels unusual or unfamiliar to the speaker; context matters.

items.example: The awards ceremony took place in glamorous surroundings.
items.note: Surroundings is normally plural for the environment around a place.

items.example: They stayed in a glamorous hotel overlooking the harbour.
items.note: A natural accommodation example illustrating the brochure adjective.

items.example: The resort provides luxurious accommodation in spacious villas.
items.note: Accommodation is usually uncountable in British English.

items.example: The luxurious cruise ship had several restaurants and pools.
items.note: Cruise ship is the vessel; cruise can mean the holiday.

items.example: We stopped for lunch in a picturesque village.
items.note: Picturesque describes a place that is visually charming, like a picture.

items.example: Narrow, picturesque streets led to the main square.
items.note: Common with places, streets, villages and cottages.

items.example: The unspoilt village retained its traditional appearance.
items.note: British spelling unspoilt; means largely unchanged or not damaged by development.

items.example: The walking route passes through unspoilt woodland.
items.note: Woodland is land covered with trees.

items.example: The exchange programme offers a unique opportunity to study abroad.
items.note: Unique means unlike any other; frequently used emphatically in adverts.

items.example: The lodge advertises unique facilities for visitors.
items.note: Facilities are services, buildings or equipment provided for a purpose.

items.pt: viajando de cruzeiro; navegando a passeio
items.example: They spent the summer cruising around the Greek islands.
items.note: The -ing form of cruise, used for leisure travel by boat.

items.example: Her fascination with ancient cities began in childhood.
items.note: Noun related to fascinating and fascinate.

items.example: The local legends fascinate visitors of all ages.
items.note: Verb related to fascination and fascinating.

items.example: The unexpected concert was a delight for everyone.
items.note: Noun and verb form related to delightful.

items.example: She felt a sense of exhilaration after finishing the climb.
items.note: Noun related to exhilarating.

items.example: The fast descent exhilarated the cyclists.
items.note: Verb meaning make someone feel excited and full of energy.

items.example: The old photographs captured the glamour of the theatre.
items.note: The noun related to glamorous, referring to an attractive, exciting style or atmosphere.

items.example: Travel adverts sometimes glamorise difficult journeys.
items.note: British -ise form; American spelling: glamorize.

items.example: For them, having a quiet room was a luxury.
items.note: Noun related to luxurious.

items.example: After the hike, we luxuriated in a long hot bath.
items.note: Verb usually followed by in; means enjoy something pleasurable fully.

items.example: We enjoyed a stunning view from the castle walls.
items.note: Stunning is an alternative to breathtaking in a positive description.

items.example: The beginner-friendly piste was clearly marked.
items.note: A prepared ski slope or route; French-derived term used in skiing.
